summary: TAIKONG is a browser-based mission design game about a lunar south pole survey crew whose base fails before the mission can begin. Players have 60 seconds to load their shuttle, then allocate limited supplies, manage crew health, and complete lunar observation work. NASA terrain and mission records inform landing-site and return-route decisions. The game lets players see how the quality of their evidence and their earlier engineering decisions affect the mission outcome.
details:
JUDGES: QUICK PLAYTHROUGH

On the title screen, select Quick Demo and enter TAIKONG-DEMO. Start the first shift, open the flight log, and use Choose tomorrow to preview a story route or daily event. Selecting the same route on later days reveals its next decision.

GAMEPLAY AND LEARNING GOALS

The crew was assigned a lunar terrain and thermal survey before the evacuation. Players decide what to load, whom to send on recovery duty, and how to ration food and water. Three interactive workstations produce survey and engineering records that can support later choices. Players can pursue a return to Earth or commission a lunar outpost.

NASA DATA IN GAMEPLAY

The return decision uses NASA Apollo 8 and Artemis I burn-to-splashdown intervals, rounded to playable days. The lunar landing decision uses published NASA LRO/LOLA slope uncertainty to model different margins for basic and detailed surveys. The analysis station compares a live game reading with a planned Artemis I flyby distance. NASA lunar illumination, ECLSS, and Deep Space Network references inform instrument and surface events. Game-specific readings and probabilities are illustrative.

TOOLS AND AUTHORSHIP

The team developed the story and design in Arcweave and implemented the game in HTML, CSS, and JavaScript. OpenAI Codex assisted with implementation, testing, research, numerical checks, language editing, artwork, and presentation preparation. A playable prototype existed before the hackathon. This version extends it with a revised mission story, observation workstations, and decision branches that use NASA data. The 60-second loading sequence was inspired by 60 Seconds!.
